analysis.one_liner: Lets striking workers collect unemployment benefits while they are on strike.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 59 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote or a House floor vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current rules, workers who go on strike generally cannot collect unemployment insurance because they are not considered unemployed and are expected to be available for work. This bill would change federal law so that workers on strike — or locked out by their employer — could receive unemployment benefits, generally starting 14 days after a strike begins, immediately if the employer locks them out or hires permanent replacements, and it would waive the usual requirements to be available for and actively seeking work. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers on strike or locked out, and the unions representing them. Today a strike means zero income for the workers, which pushes people back to work quickly and shortens strikes. Unemployment benefits would give striking workers a paycheck stream, letting them hold out longer, and would also cover workers who cannot work as an indirect result of a labor dispute, such as employees of a supplier whose plant shut down because of a strike elsewhere.

how_it_helps.text: Workers unable to work because of a labor dispute would be treated as if they were unemployed and could collect unemployment compensation.
Benefits would begin 14 days after a strike starts, immediately upon a lockout, immediately if the employer hires permanent replacement workers, or when the dispute ends, whichever is earliest.
Striking workers would be exempt from the federal requirement that unemployment claimants be able to work, available for work, and actively seeking work.
The protection extends to workers unable to work as an indirect result of a labor dispute, not just the striking employees themselves.

analysis.who_pays: State unemployment insurance systems, which are funded by payroll taxes on employers, would bear the cost of paying benefits during strikes and would likely need higher tax collections to cover them. Employers facing strikes would also lose their current advantage: workers with an income stream can sustain picket lines longer, making strikes a bigger economic threat to the company.

drawbacks.text: State unemployment insurance trust funds, many of which borrowed from the federal government after being depleted during the pandemic, would absorb the added cost of paying benefits to workers who are technically employed, potentially requiring higher unemployment payroll taxes on all employers.

Because benefits would flow to people who are still employed, the bill would weaken the traditional link between unemployment insurance and involuntary joblessness, and employers would argue it publicly subsidizes strikes and lengthens labor disputes.
The bill addresses the money problem of striking but not the underlying disputes; benefits could extend confrontations between unions and employers rather than resolve them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For striking workers the benefit is direct and substantial: a strike today means losing all income, which is why strikes are so hard to sustain. The cost falls on state unemployment systems and, through payroll taxes, on employers broadly, and there is a fair argument that paying unemployment benefits to people who still have jobs blurs the program's purpose. The bill never received a committee or floor vote, so there was no refined version or cost estimate to weigh; as introduced, it is a real income guarantee for strikers paid for by employers and state UI funds.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for its entire life — the committee never acted on it, and at the very end of the Congress it was sent to a subcommittee — so it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on October 25, 2023, with 40 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill accumulated 59 Democratic cosponsors in total, but no Republicans signed on.
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action for more than a year; on December 17, 2024, with the Congress weeks from ending, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare.
No committee vote, floor vote, or Senate action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing strikes — and any members opposed to public support for strikers — are better off, because keeping the bill in committee meant workers on strike still have no income and strikes remain short. Striking workers gained nothing.

for.name: Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let striking workers collect unemployment benefits.

for.name: 59 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 59 cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Jason Smith, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat for over a year and was referred to a subcommittee only in the final weeks of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic: the sponsor plus 59 cosponsors were all House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors and no Republican-led committee action.

industries.industry: Employers facing strikes (manufacturers, logistics, hospitals, and other unionized workplaces)
industries.note: Striking workers with unemployment income can hold out much longer, so strikes become a more credible and costly threat, and the employer's ability to wait out a walkout shrinks — especially since benefits kick in immediately if it hires permanent replacements.

industries.industry: State unemployment insurance systems and their employer payroll-tax base
industries.note: The bill adds a new class of claimants to funds financed by employer payroll taxes, raising system costs and likely unemployment taxes broadly; those costs fund an income guarantee for striking workers.
Longer, more sustainable strikes are a union's main leverage in bargaining; an income stream for strikers strengthens it, and the bill also covers workers idled indirectly by a dispute.
